In adhering to this structure, your objective is: 
        Propose up to three reusable lessons for your assigned role from trusted feedback.
        
        Preserve previous useful strategies. Do not copy patient facts, quotations,
        sentence/study IDs or case-specific clinical rules into the rule text. Only use
        supporting episode IDs from the provided trusted feedback. Never require an
        original/control report at Blue inference. Red must seek clinically plausible
        image errors, not parser exploits. Blue must improve error detection while
        preserving supported claims, rather than abstaining on everything. Feedback
        is fallible model consensus, not clinician ground truth. Only your own role's
        inputs and feedback are available. Return [] if evidence warrants no new lesson.

[[ ## role ## ]]
blue

["When a vision tool explicitly states the absence of a finding (e.g., 'No definite focal consolidation, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax is identified'), and the candidate report explicitly claims the presence of that finding, confidently flag it as a contradiction, even if other vision tool observations are less definitive or conflicting.", "When an observation from a vision tool explicitly identifies a finding (e.g., a calcified nodule or cardiomegaly), and the candidate report explicitly denies or contradicts this finding, confidently flag it as a contradiction.", "Do not overlook significant discrepancies or fabricated findings in the candidate report, such as the addition of a pneumothorax, even if the primary focus of the vision tool observations was on other findings like cardiomegaly or pulmonary artery hypertension.", "Avoid flagging the absence of a finding when subtle image features suggest its possible presence.", "When image quality or views are limited, prioritize uncertainty and avoid confident error flags.", "Do not confidently flag a claim as incorrect if the image findings are open to multiple interpretations.", "Acknowledge limitations of single-view radiographs when assessing findings.", "Be cautious when assessing subtle differences in image density, especially when characterizing opacities.", "Do not allow general limitations of plain radiographs (e.g., difficulty with precise localization or subtle findings) to prevent flagging clear contradictions when a specific finding is visible and explicitly denied by the candidate."]
